Deficient Squares

DivisibilityAreaInduction
Game: One square of the board is missing. Cover every other square with L-shaped pieces of three squares.
How to play: Pick any size from 2 × 2 to 24 × 24, then click three free squares in an L, each next to the one before. Use Remove last when you trap yourself.

Look for the math

Golomb's theorem covers boards of side 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. This page asks the same question for a square board of any side, from 2 to 24, with one square removed. Some sizes and some gaps cannot be covered at all, and this page lets you see why. A board with one square missing is called deficient; the pieces are L-trominoes.

Three squares at a time

Every L covers exactly 3 squares, so a tiling can only exist when the number of squares left is a multiple of 3. An n × n board has n² squares, so the gap leaves n² − 1. When n is a multiple of 3, n² is too, and n² − 1 is one less: it leaves remainder 2, never 0. Sizes 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24 are therefore impossible, whatever square is missing. When n is not a multiple of 3, n² − 1 is a multiple of 3, and the count alone no longer forbids a tiling. This is arithmetic modulo 3.

The 5 × 5 surprise

Counting is necessary but not sufficient. On a 5 × 5 board, 24 squares are left, enough for 8 pieces, yet only 9 of the 25 possible gaps work: the four corners and the centre, the squares whose row and column are both even. Every other gap leaves a shape that no set of Ls can cover. The logic test searches all 25 gaps and confirms exactly those 9.

The cut-the-knot page states the theorem as "if n ≥ 5, a deficient n × n board tiles if and only if n is not a multiple of 3". The 5 × 5 board shows that this is not quite right as written. From 7 × 7 upward the statement does hold: the test searches every gap up to 7 × 7, and the theorem of I-Ping Chu and Richard Johnsonbaugh covers the rest. A 5 × 5 board is the one exception, and its corner case is what the general proof starts from.

Why every larger board works

For sides that are powers of 2 the proof is Golomb's: split the board into four quarters, put one L round the centre covering the three quarters without the gap, and repeat inside each quarter. For a general side the proof is again induction, but on n rather than on the exponent. The small cases are checked by hand — the 5 × 5 corner tiling is one essential brick — and a board of side n is then reduced to one of side n − 3, so that all the sides with the same remainder modulo 3 follow together.

Pockets

During play the same counting argument is your warning. An L takes 3 squares, so the number still to cover always has the same remainder modulo 3 as when you started. A pocket of one or two squares can never be filled: no L fits, and the count will not come out right. That is what the page means by "1 and 2 squares pockets". Remove last takes pieces back until the pocket merges with free space.

Try a 5 × 5 board and move the gap with Set blank. Only the four corners and the centre can be tiled, and the centre is much harder than a corner. Then try 7 × 7: every gap works, but a bad first piece can still strand the rest.
